e.etymology: A recent American coinage that joins Scott, or Scotland, to the popular -lyn ending, on the pattern of Brooklyn and Oaklyn.
e.note: Sounds almost the same as Scotland, so some people will hear the country.

e.etymology: A form of Quentin, from Latin Quintinus, built on Quintus, fifth, a name Romans gave a fifth child. Saint Quentin, a 3rd-century martyr, spread it through France.
A pet form of Edward, Edgar, Edwin and other names beginning with Ed-, from Old English ead, wealth or fortune. Eddie is the more common spelling.

assoc.t: eddy, a small whirlpool in water or air

e.etymology: From the English adjective stormy. It has been given as a name in the United States since the mid-1900s, alongside Storm.
namesakes: Stormy Daniels (adult film actress in the Trump hush-money case)

assoc.t: Stormy Daniels, adult film star in Trump hush-money case

e.note: Many adults will think first of Stormy Daniels, the adult film actress at the center of Donald Trump's hush-money trial.

e.etymology: In India from Sanskrit nila, dark blue, and in Tamil a word for the moon. It is also the Russian feminine of Nil, and older American use is linked to the name Nile.
Coined in Missouri in 1877 by the mother of Sedona Schnebly, who liked the sound. The Arizona town was named for Schnebly in 1902 when her husband opened its post office.

assoc.t: Sedona, Arizona, red-rock resort town
Kia Sedona minivan, sold in the US until 2021

e.etymology: From the English word verity, truth, from Latin veritas. It is one of the virtue names the Puritans adopted in the 17th century and has stayed in use in Britain.

assoc.t: Verity, Colleen Hoover's bestselling thriller novel

e.etymology: The Arabic form of Jonah, from Hebrew yonah, dove, by way of Greek Ionas. Yunus is a prophet in the Quran, where a chapter bears his name.
namesakes: Yunus Musah (US national soccer team midfielder)

e.etymology: A modern American name with no documented source. It follows the sound of Kiara and of the -ari names such as Amari and Kamari.
From Hindi dev, from Sanskrit deva, a god or divine being, a word related to Latin deus. It is also a short form of longer names such as Devdas and Devendra.
namesakes: Dev Patel (star of Slumdog Millionaire and Lion)

assoc.t: dev, tech shorthand for a software developer

e.etymology: A modern American spelling of Kyree, a name in the family of Tyree and Kyrie. No older source is documented.
From the Roman family name Caecilius, from Latin caecus, blind. English use follows the noble Cecil family, whose surname comes from the Old Welsh name Seisyllt, itself from Latin Sextilius.
namesakes: Cecil B. DeMille (director of The Ten Commandments)
Cecil Rhodes (British imperialist and Rhodes Scholarship founder)

assoc.t: Cecil the lion, killed by a trophy hunter in 2015

e.etymology: From an English surname that began as a medieval pet form of Emma, a Germanic name meaning whole or universal. Irish families also use it in honor of the patriot Robert Emmet.
namesakes: Emmet Brickowski (hero of The Lego Movie)

assoc.t: Emmet, the hero of The Lego Movie

e.etymology: From the Irish surname Mag Fhionnain, son of Fionnan, a pet form of fionn, fair or white. Its use as a first name is modern and mostly American.

assoc.t: Ganon, villain of The Legend of Zelda (same sound)

e.etymology: An American coinage that joins Kent to the -rell ending of Terrell and Darrell. Rapper YoungBoy Never Broke Again, born Kentrell Gaulden, raised its profile in the late 2010s.
namesakes: YoungBoy Never Broke Again (rapper, born Kentrell Gaulden)

assoc.t: Kentrell, given name of rapper YoungBoy Never Broke Again

e.etymology: From Arabic Zakariyya, the Quranic form of Hebrew Zekharyah, the Lord has remembered. In the Quran and the Gospels he is the father of John the Baptist.

assoc.t: Fareed Zakaria, CNN host and columnist (surname)

e.etymology: A form of Adelia and Adela, from the Germanic element adal, noble. A separate Adalia appears in the Book of Esther as one of the sons of Haman.
From Old French Gerart, from Frankish words for spear and for hard or brave. The Normans brought it to England, and several medieval saints kept it in use.

From Roma, the Latin and Italian name of the city of Rome. English speakers took it up as a girls' name in the late 1800s; in Russia Roma is a pet form of Roman, and in India it is a separate Hindu name.
namesakes: Roma Downey (star of Touched by an Angel)

assoc.t: Roma, the Italian name for Rome
Roma, the Romani people of Europe
Roma tomato, the common plum tomato
Roma, Alfonso Cuaron's Oscar-winning 2018 film
AS Roma, Italian soccer club

e.etymology: A short form of Kipling, an English surname taken from a place name. Americans have given it as a full name since the mid-1900s.
namesakes: Kip Dynamite (Napoleon's brother in Napoleon Dynamite)

assoc.t: kip, British slang for a nap

e.etymology: From Greek myth: Danae was the princess of Argos whom Zeus visited as a shower of gold, and the mother of the hero Perseus. The name is tied to the Danaans, an old name for the Greeks.
From the English word story, which goes back through Old French to Latin historia. Story is also an old English surname, and parents began using the word as a first name in the 2000s.

assoc.t: story, the everyday word for a tale

e.etymology: From Old Norse Ivarr, built from words for yew, the wood of bows, and for warrior. Ivar the Boneless led the Viking army that invaded England in 865.
namesakes: Ivar the Boneless (Viking leader, a lead character in TV's Vikings)

assoc.t: Ivar the Boneless of the TV series Vikings

e.etymology: From an English surname brought by a Norman family called d'Airel, from Airelle in Calvados, France. It became a first name in the 19th century and peaked in the 1950s.
From the Italian surname De Angelo, of Angelo, a name meaning angel or messenger. Black American families also formed it afresh from the De- prefix and Angelo in the late 20th century.
namesakes: DeAngelo Vickers (Will Ferrell's character on The Office)

e.etymology: From Arabic faris, a horseman or knight, from faras, horse. It is used across the Arab world and among Bosnian and Southeast Asian Muslims.
A modern American coinage that joins the Jay sound to the -lyn ending. It is one of many spellings alongside Jaelyn, Jaylin and Jaylyn.
e.note: The spelling begins with the word jail, which may draw comments or teasing.

e.etymology: A spelling of Casey, from the Irish surname O Cathasaigh, descendant of Cathasach, a byname meaning vigilant. The K and -i spellings spread in the United States in the 1980s.
A modern American spelling of Alexander that writes out the z sound and the nickname Zander. Alexander is from Greek Alexandros, from alexein, to defend, and aner, man.
e.note: The standard spelling Alexander is far more common, so expect to spell this one out.

e.etymology: A modern American name with no documented source. It appears to join the Ty- sound to Amir or Jamir, and it resembles Timur and Tamir.

e.meaning: keeper of a forest or park
e.etymology: From the English word ranger, first a warden who patrolled a royal forest, and from the occupational surname it produced. Its use as a first name is recent.

assoc.t: park ranger or forest ranger
Ford Ranger pickup truck
Texas Rangers (MLB) and New York Rangers (NHL)
Army Rangers, elite US Army infantry
Power Rangers and the Lone Ranger

e.etymology: From an English surname of Norman origin, taken from Caillouet in Normandy, a place named for its pebbles, Old French caillou. Its use as a first name is recent.

assoc.t: Callaway, golf club and ball maker
Cab Calloway, jazz bandleader (spelled Calloway)
